lines.text: In an age of screens, it may seem strange that anyone still keeps
a diary on paper. Yet many people, young and old, continues to write
lines.note: Agreement: 'many people' is plural, so it is 'continue'.

lines.text: in a notebook every night. Some say that writing by hand slows them
down and helps them thinking more clearly. Others like knowing that nobody else
lines.note: Verb form: after 'helps them' the verb stays plain — 'think'.

lines.text: can read his private thoughts. A paper diary cannot be hacked, and it
lines.note: Pronoun: 'others' is plural, so it is 'their'.

lines.text: needs neither a password or a battery. There is also a simple pleasure
in choosing a pen and filling a clean page with one’s own handwrite.
lines.note: Word form: after 'one’s own' a noun is needed — 'handwriting'.

lines.text: Years later, the pages become a record of who the writer once was.
My aunt has kept a diary since she is fourteen, and she owns
lines.note: Tense: she was fourteen in the past, so it is 'was'.

lines.text: more than thirty notebook today. She says that reading the oldest ones is
like meeting a youngest version of herself. Typing may be faster, but for
lines.note: Comparative: she is comparing two selves, so it is 'a younger version'.

lines.text: people like her, nothing can replace the feel of ink on paper.
